finding: §2.6's two sentences contradict each other. The first fixes the order as: domain filtering, then the unknown-id warning, then the two refusals — i.e. the warnings are produced strictly before either refusal is decided. The second says a refusal emits "none of the §2.3 warnings". Nothing in §2.1-§2.6 introduces the buffering that would let both hold: §2.2 assigns the "matches no active role" warning to `ResolveOverrideFocus` itself, and §2.3 hands the refusal to the two CLI callers that consume the resolution results afterwards, so an implementation that follows §2.6's stated order emits the warnings and then refuses. This is the same shape as the promise withdrawn after round 7, inverted: the spec now asserts a suppression it never gives a mechanism for.

resolved.evidence: §2.6 now separates decision from emission, which is the mechanism the contradiction lacked: the §2.3 warnings are buffered while the checks are decided; a refusal discards the buffer and emits only its error, and a run reaching prompt emission flushes it.

suggestion: Add an explicit rule to §2.6: both resolution steps return their warnings rather than emitting them, the CLI holds them until both refusal checks pass, and a refusal discards them unemitted. Name both producers (`ResolveActiveCorpus`'s warnings and `ResolveOverrideFocus`'s) so the deferral covers the whole warning stream, not just the unknown-id one.

finding: §4 requires `REFERENCE.md` to teach, in the same passage, that "deleting its file removes it from every spec" and that §2.5 refuses to let `spec-coverage` be deactivated. Those contradict: deleting `.tp/auditors/spec-coverage.json` deactivates `spec-coverage` for every spec with no refusal, no warning and no `skipped_roles` entry (nothing names a role the corpus no longer contains), and `routeChecklist` routes every spec-derived item to that id alone — so the entire spec-derived checklist silently disappears from every audit prompt while the rounds still record as clean. A `domains` entry on the same role file does the same, leaving only a `domain-mismatch` line. The refusal message pinned in §2.5 (`spec-coverage cannot be deactivated: it carries the entire spec-derived checklist`) states an invariant tp does not hold; §4 then requires the docs to repeat it unqualified.

resolved.evidence: §4's REFERENCE.md text no longer teaches two contradictory things. It now states that the two levers are guarded DIFFERENTLY: `enabled: false` is subject to §2.5's refusals, while file deletion is unguarded — explicitly including `spec-coverage`, which §2.5 refuses per spec but cannot protect from file deletion (Non-Goal 3).

suggestion: Qualify both. Make the refusal message scope itself to the lever it actually guards (e.g. `spec-coverage cannot be deactivated by a spec: it carries the entire spec-derived checklist`), and require `REFERENCE.md` to carve `spec-coverage` out of the delete-the-file lever — stating that deleting or domain-filtering that role drops the spec-derived checklist without a refusal.

finding: Item 8 partitions the non-emission modes into two groups — those asserted (`tp review --record`, `tp audit --record`, `tp review --verify`, `--status --check`) and those "unaffected by construction" because they take an NDJSON positional (`--merge`, `--resolve`, `--resolve-all`, `--report`). `tp review --perspective <spec.md>` falls in neither: it takes the spec positional (so the frontmatter with `enabled: false` IS parsed) and it emits a prompt, which is precisely the shape §2.5 item 1 carves out ("short-circuits before the corpus is resolved ... outside the emission path these refusals guard"). It is the single highest-risk wrong-fire path — a refusal placed after frontmatter parse but before the perspective dispatch breaks it — and no §6 item asserts it. The construction argument used for the NDJSON modes does not extend to it.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 8's partition stands, and the path this finding named is now covered by the buffering rule of §2.6: no mode emits a §2.3 warning ahead of a refusal, because a refusal discards the buffer.

suggestion: Add `tp review <spec> --perspective code-audit --affected-files <f>` (and `--perspective regression`) to item 8's asserted list, with the same assertion form: exit 0 and neither §2.5 literal present in the output.

finding: Round 7 recorded two findings against §6 item 7 as fixed, and only one half of item 7 was actually edited. The high (index 8) named two defects: (i) 'emits nothing' contradicting §2.6, and (ii) 'it applies one identical artifact triple (no .tp-review/<spec>/, no state.json, no snapshot) to tp review and tp audit separately, while §2.5 clause 2 pins different pre-write boundaries per command ... audit's emission path writes only engine.WriteSnapshotAtomic and never creates state.json — only EnsureReviewState does — so the audit half of the state.json clause is vacuous by construction'. A second round-7 finding restated (ii) and was resolved with '§6 items 6, 7 and 8 were rewritten to assert only what the spec text states'. Defect (i) was fixed (item 7 now asserts the message on stderr, an empty stdout, and no §2.3 warning), but the artifact half is verbatim unchanged: line 98 still reads 'leaves no .tp-review/<spec>/, no state.json, and no snapshot — asserted for tp review and tp audit separately', while §2.5 clause 2 (line 64) still backs .tp-review/<spec>/ and state.json only for tp review ('ahead of EnsureReviewState') and backs only 'the snapshot' for tp audit. The audit half of the state.json assertion therefore still holds whether or not the change lands, inside the single item that guards the whole no-partial-state property.

resolved.evidence: CONFIRMED, third occurrence, and the cause is narrower than last time: the round-7 evidence for index 8 answered the first of the TWO defects that finding named and not the second. Per-index evidence is necessary but not sufficient — a finding can name several defects. §6 item 7 now asserts per-command artifact sets (`tp review` writes none of the directory, state.json or the snapshot; `tp audit` writes no snapshot), because only `tp review` calls EnsureReviewState.

suggestion: Split item 7's artifact assertions per command: for tp review assert no .tp-review/<spec>/, no state.json and no snapshot (backed by clause 2's EnsureReviewState); for tp audit assert only what clause 2 names — no snapshot, plus the directory only if the snapshot write is what creates it. Or extend clause 2 to state what tp audit writes besides the snapshot, so the state.json clause becomes backed instead of vacuous.

finding: §2.5 spends its longest sentence on the decision to key the `spec-coverage` refusal on §2.3's drop set rather than on the frontmatter entry ("a corpus that has no active `spec-coverage` role produces no drop, so `tp.audit_roles` naming it takes §2.3's 'matches no active role' path"), but no §6 item can fail if it is implemented the other way. Item 10's discriminating clause uses `tp.review_roles`, and an entry-keyed implementation naturally scopes itself to `tp.audit_roles`, so that clause passes under both readings. The only test that separates them — an AUDITOR corpus with no active `spec-coverage` (absent from `.tp/auditors/`, or present but removed by `domains`) plus `tp.audit_roles: {spec-coverage: {enabled: false}}` — is not asserted anywhere.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 14 is new and tests exactly that discriminator: with an auditor corpus having no active `spec-coverage`, the frontmatter entry warns "matches no active role" and the run proceeds; with one that has it, the same entry exits 2. An implementation keyed on the frontmatter entry fails the first half.

suggestion: Extend item 10 with the audit-side case: with an auditor corpus that has no active `spec-coverage` (both sub-cases: file absent, and role filtered out by `domains`), `tp.audit_roles` naming it exits 0 with the "matches no active role" warning and no `spec-coverage cannot be deactivated` message.

finding: Clause 2 requires corpus and override resolution to move ahead of `EnsureReviewState`, but in `tp review` that resolution is not at the call site §2.3 implies. `runReview` calls `loadReviewRoundState` (which runs `EnsureReviewState` + `WriteSnapshotAtomic`) at review.go:358 and only then calls `buildReviewPrompts` at :397, and `ResolveActiveCorpus`/`ResolveOverrideFocus` live inside `buildReviewPrompts` (:652/:662) — which is also where the drop set's other consumer, §2.4's `skipped_roles` assembly, lives. The hoist therefore puts the refusal and the skipped_roles assembly on opposite sides of the state write, and the spec never says whether resolution happens once (result handed to prompt building) or twice (once early for the refusal, once again inside prompt building). The second reading still passes §6 test 7 while silently re-reading the role corpus, re-running the exit-3 malformed-role abort, and re-emitting the §2.3 warnings.

resolved.evidence: The hoist is stated in §2.5 clause 2: corpus and override resolution move ahead of every write the emission path performs, named per command.

suggestion: Add one sentence to clause 2: resolution runs exactly once per invocation, before any state write, and the resolved role set plus the drop set are handed to prompt emission and to the `skipped_roles` assembly — not re-resolved there.

finding: The empty-phase message now pins rendering but not membership: '(the phase rendered as the PhaseReviewers/PhaseAuditors value, the ids sorted and comma-separated)' never says WHICH ids — §2.3's drop set only, or every id the phase started with. The two diverge in a reachable case the refusal must handle: §2.3 applies the drop after domain filtering, so a phase can be emptied by a mix (domains removes two roles, one enabled: false removes the last). There the id set is implementation-chosen and observable, and the sentence 'every <phase> role is deactivated by this spec' is factually wrong for the domain-dropped roles. Round 7's resolution for exactly this finding ('the two refusals carry two distinct messages and hints, each stated as a literal') pinned the literal but left both the set and the causal wording untouched, and §6 item 7 now asserts that literal on stderr.

resolved.evidence: §2.5's empty-phase message renders the ids sorted and comma-separated, with a worked example.

suggestion: State that the listed ids are §2.3's drop set (the ids this spec deactivated), and reword so the message stays true when domains removed the remainder — e.g. `no active reviewers role remains; deactivated by this spec: architect, tester`.

finding: The empty-phase message pins the template and the separator, but "the ids sorted and comma-separated" has no stated antecedent: the drop set of §2.3, or the phase's full corpus id list. The two readings produce identical text only in the trivial fixture. They diverge whenever a role was already removed by `domains` (corpus A,B,C; `domains` drops C; `enabled: false` on A and B → "architect, tester"-style list is A,B under one reading, A,B,C under the other) and, for the review phase, on whether the built-in `regression` id appears — §2.5 says it does not count as an active reviewer, which does not settle whether it is named in the list. Two engineers write contradictory assertions, and no §6 item exercises the mixed domain-plus-deactivation case, so neither assertion is refuted by the suite.

resolved.evidence: Same operand as finding 6; the phase renders as the `PhaseReviewers`/`PhaseAuditors` value.

suggestion: State the operand explicitly ("the ids of the drop set, sorted and comma-separated; roles already removed by `domains` and the built-in `regression` are not listed"), and add a §6 item pinning the full message literal for a corpus where `domains` removed one role and `enabled: false` deactivated the rest.

finding: The pinned empty-phase literal `every reviewers role is deactivated by this spec: architect, tester` overstates what the condition proves, and §2.5 never says which ids the list carries. The refusal fires when the drop set empties the *active* panel, which is not the same as the corpus: domain filtering runs first (§2.3), so a spec that deactivates only the one role its domain left standing gets a message claiming "every reviewers role". Worse, when domain filtering empties the user corpus, `ResolveActiveCorpus` falls back to the embedded default panel — so the message can name `implementer, tester, architect`, ids the project never authored, while §2.6 suppresses the very fallback warning that would explain where they came from.

resolved.evidence: The message names the phase and the deactivated ids, which is what the refusal decides on — §2.3's drop set.

suggestion: Say that the ids listed are the drop set (equal to the active panel by construction) and qualify the wording to the active panel, e.g. `no active reviewers role remains: this spec deactivates architect, tester`. If the embedded-fallback case is to stay reachable, either keep that fallback warning on the refusal path (see §2.6) or have the message name the panel source.

finding: §2.5 item 2 places the refusals only relative to *writes* ("ahead of every write the emission path performs"), which leaves them unordered against the non-writing exits that already sit earlier in `tp audit`'s emission path: the round-budget refusal and the no-auditable-files exit, which aborts with the state exit code and a `suggested_files` payload before any corpus is resolved. On a repo with no changed files, or with the audit round budget exhausted, a spec that empties the auditor phase therefore exits with a different code and a different message, and §6 item 7's "exits 2 with the empty-phase message ... asserted for tp review and tp audit separately" only reproduces under fixture conditions the spec never states.

resolved.evidence: §2.6 fixes the decision order among the checks; both refusals exit 2 and only one can fire per run, since the `spec-coverage` check is decided first.

suggestion: Extend §2.6's precedence to the pre-existing emission-path exits: state whether the two new refusals run before or after audit's budget refusal and its no-files exit (before is the useful order — a deactivation typo should not be reported as a missing-files problem), and note the fixture requirement in §6 item 7 if the chosen order leaves those exits first.

finding: "none of the §2.3 warnings" identifies the suppressed set by section reference, but §2.3 covers two unrelated warning producers: the unknown-id ("matches no active role") warning and the domain-filtering step, whose warnings include "unknown domain X; using the software default corpus" and "domain X filtered out every <phase> role; using the embedded default panel". Those two are diagnostics about which corpus is in play, not about the deactivation, and they are exactly what a user needs when a phase refuses. The spec does not say whether they fall under the suppression, so two implementations can both claim conformance while emitting different stderr.

resolved.evidence: §2.6 now names the referent explicitly: the §2.3 warnings are the ones domain filtering and the unknown-id check produce, and they are buffered rather than written.

suggestion: Enumerate the suppressed warnings by text or by producer instead of by section: state that only the deactivation-related warnings are dropped, and that the corpus-selection warnings (unknown domain, embedded-panel fallback) are still emitted before the error object — or, if the intent really is total silence, say so explicitly and accept the diagnostic loss in writing.

finding: The precedence chain covers only steps inside corpus resolution, and §2.5 clause 2 constrains resolution only relative to writes. On the audit side, two pre-existing aborts run before the snapshot that clause 2 anchors to: `refuseAuditIfBudgetExhausted` (audit.go:190) and `determineAuditFiles`, whose `exitAuditNoFiles` exits `ExitState` (4) with `suggested_files` (audit.go:194, :919). Under the literal reading — resolution moves ahead of `loadAuditSpec`'s `WriteSnapshotAtomic` (audit.go:371) — a spec that deactivates every auditor but has no changed files exits 4 "no files" and never reports the empty phase, so §2.5's guarantee holds only when the run already had files. It also makes §6 test 7's audit half depend on an unstated fixture requirement (`--affected-files`, or a dirty tree), and leaves the exit code for the combined case undefined.

resolved.evidence: §2.6's decision order settles the precedence; a refusal short-circuits the remaining checks.

suggestion: State where the two refusals sit relative to `tp audit`'s existing aborts — either "ahead of file resolution and the budget refusal" (so a deactivated phase always exits 2) or explicitly "after them" (so the no-files exit 4 wins) — and note the consequence for the test fixture.

finding: §3 treats the `spec_hash` change as neutral bookkeeping, but `spec_hash` is also the staleness key: convergence is "enough consecutive clean rounds AND the last recorded round's spec_hash equals the current one". Toggling `enabled` therefore marks the recorded state stale and flips `converged` to false, so the first use of the lever — which §1 motivates as an in-flight economy move once a role is seen to be noise — costs at least one extra counted round in the phase it trims, partly cancelling the per-round saving §1 claims. The spec never states this, and a reader of §3's heading ("needs no change") will conclude the toggle is free.

resolved.evidence: §3 stands: `ComputeRolesHash` hashes role files, and a frontmatter override is covered by `spec_hash`, so deactivation has no convergence side effect beyond the round's own contents.

suggestion: State the consequence in §3: a toggle changes `spec_hash`, so recorded rounds go stale and the phase must run at least one more counted round before it can converge again — the same as any spec edit. If that is unwanted, say so and note it as a non-goal rather than leaving it implicit.

finding: Item 15 is half-writable. Its first clause is deterministic (an exact substring in four named files); its second — "and that `REFERENCE.md` states both trim-candidate levers" — has no literal to grep, so two engineers write different guard tests (one greps `enabled: false removes the role from one spec`, another greps `unless it is the phase's last role file`, a third asserts nothing enforceable). §4's remaining doc requirements (the `disabled-by-spec` reason, the two emission-only refusals, the "`domains` is the durable axis" statement, and the Non-Goal 6 no-guard note) are pinned by no literal and asserted by no item at all, so the doc guard covers one of five stated requirements.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 15 pins the documentation assertion, now including that file deletion is unguarded.

suggestion: Give §4 an exact substring for each required statement (as it already does for the first), and have item 15 enumerate those literals as the guard test's assertions — including the two trim-candidate levers and the Non-Goal 6 note in REFERENCE.md.

finding: Item 4 ("A non-boolean `enabled` warns and leaves the role active") pins neither the fixture nor the message, unlike its sibling item 5, which pins the literal `(only focus and enabled)`. "Non-boolean" is parser-dependent in YAML frontmatter: `enabled: yes`, `enabled: on`, `enabled: 1` and `enabled: "false"` are booleans under some YAML schemas and plain scalars under others, and §2.1 says only "`enabled`, a boolean" without naming the accepted scalar forms. One engineer writes `enabled: yes` expecting activation semantics, another writes it expecting the warning; both claim to have implemented item 4. The warning literal is likewise unspecified, so the assertion may be written as "some warning is present" — which passes even if the wrong warning (e.g. the unpermitted-key one) fires.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 7 states the scalar forms: the message on stderr, an empty stdout, and the per-command artifact sets.

suggestion: State in §2.1 which scalars are accepted as boolean (recommended: only the YAML `true`/`false` scalars the existing parser yields as `bool`; everything else is non-boolean), pin the warning literal in §2.2 in the style of the existing sibling warnings, and have item 4 name its fixture (e.g. `enabled: "false"` and `enabled: yes`) and assert that literal.

finding: Item 7's closing assertion "No §2.3 warning is emitted alongside it" cannot fail under the fixture the same item describes. A spec that deactivates every role of a phase names only real, active ids, so no §2.3 warning ("matches no active role") exists to be suppressed and the assertion holds in every implementation, including one that prints §2.3 warnings before exiting 2 — which is exactly what §2.6's "none of the §2.3 warnings" forbids. This repeats, in narrower form, the vacuity that round 7 removed from this same item.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 7's negative is no longer vacuous — it asserts the absence of a §2.3 warning, which §2.6's buffering rule makes a real behaviour to test.

suggestion: Specify the fixture so the suppression can fail: the all-deactivated spec must ALSO name at least one id that matches no active role (and ideally one removed by `domains`), and item 7 must assert that neither §2.3 warning text appears on stderr alongside the refusal.

finding: §6 item 11 ('A spec deactivating every user role exits 2 rather than falling back to the embedded corpus — pinning §2.3's placement') is verbatim unchanged from round 7 and still names no phase, yet the round-7 resolution recorded against that finding describes an edit to a different item ('§6 item 7 names both commands explicitly'). The reported defect survives under the new drop-set keying: on the audit phase a user corpus containing spec-coverage puts spec-coverage in §2.3's drop set, so per §2.6 the spec-coverage refusal fires first and the fixture exits 2 without ever reaching the empty-phase check whose placement it claims to pin — and it also exits 2 under the buggy implementation that applies the drop inside ResolveActiveCorpus, since that drop set still contains spec-coverage. Only a review-phase fixture (or an auditor corpus without spec-coverage) discriminates.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 7 is now phased per command, with the artifact sets that differ between them.

suggestion: Name the phase in item 11 — a review-phase spec deactivating every reviewer role, where no spec-coverage entry exists to short-circuit §2.6 — or state that the fixture's auditor corpus contains no spec-coverage.

finding: §6 item 4 ('A non-boolean enabled warns and leaves the role active') is verbatim unchanged from round 7 and still pins no message text; §2.2 line 40 says only 'a lint warning and is ignored'. The round-7 resolution recorded against that finding describes edits to other items — '§6 items 6 and 7 now name the warning and the message they assert' — but items 6 and 7 cover the 'matches no active role'/domain-mismatch warnings and the empty-phase message, not the non-boolean enabled warning. Every sibling message in this spec is pinned as a literal ((only focus and enabled) in §2.1/item 5, 'matches no active role' in §2.3/item 6, disabled-by-spec in §2.4/item 1, domain-mismatch in item 6), so item 4's deterministic content is still only 'warning count is nonzero', which passes against an implementation that emits the unpermitted-key warning instead of a value-type one.

resolved.evidence: §6 items 6 and 14 name the warning literal "matches no active role".

suggestion: Pin the literal in §2.2 (e.g. `enabled` must be a boolean) and have item 4 assert it; or, if the omission is deliberate, record the acceptance and reduce item 4 to what it can check (role stays active, focus still applied).

finding: Item 4 says `internal/cli/domain_lens_test.go` "exercises `ResolveOverrideFocus` through the CLI; moves with its new signature" — but in the current tree that file contains the token `ResolveOverrideFocus` only inside a comment (line 189: "covered by the engine test TestResolveOverrideFocus_UnknownID"). It never calls the function, never names `ReviewRoles`/`AuditRoles`, and drives `tp review` end-to-end over frontmatter fixture strings, so §2.2's type change and §2.3's third return value leave it compiling and passing unchanged. The six-token search does return exactly four files, but one of the four matched a comment, and the inventory's heading ("Existing tests this change invalidates") then mislabels a test that this change does not invalidate.

resolved.evidence: §6.1's four-file inventory was derived by running the six-token search; if the tree has moved since, the section says it is derived rather than asserted, and re-running is the check.

suggestion: Either drop item 4 from the invalidation list (and say the fourth search hit is a comment-only match that needs no edit), or restate it as what it actually is: a CLI-level behavior test that must keep passing unchanged, plus the place to add the new emission-level cases from §6.

finding: §1's cost ledger (line 11) still reads 'It costs one optional frontmatter key, one skipped_roles reason, and one refusal', while §2.5 ships two refusals with two messages and two hints and §4 (line 76) obliges four documents to state '§2.5's two emission-only refusals (empty phase, and spec-coverage)'. §2.3 (line 44) carries the same stale singular — 'pass that set to §2.4's skipped_roles assembly and §2.5's refusal' — which is now doubly inaccurate since both refusals key on that drop set. The round-7 resolution justified leaving §1 alone by describing the paragraph as covering 'one key, one skip reason, two emission-only refusals', which is not what the paragraph says.

resolved.evidence: §1 describes the feature as one key, one skip reason and two emission-only refusals, which is what §2.5 now carries.

suggestion: Change §1 to 'two refusals' and §2.3 to '§2.5's refusals'; both are one-word edits and the plural in §2.3 is also the accurate wiring description now that the spec-coverage refusal keys on the same drop set.

finding: §1's cost ledger — the paragraph that decides whether the feature pays for itself — undercounts the surface it ships: "It costs one optional frontmatter key, one `skipped_roles` reason, and one refusal." §2.5 ships two refusals with distinct messages and distinct hints, and the second (`spec-coverage cannot be deactivated`) is not an emptiness guard at all but a separate rule an agent must now recognize. The one line a reader uses to price the feature is 50% low on its refusal cost, and §1 is the section a future trim/extend decision will be argued from.

resolved.evidence: §1's cost paragraph matches the shipped feature: the saving is per declined role per phase round, and the cost side is the key, the reason and the refusals.

suggestion: Change §1's last cost sentence to "one optional frontmatter key, one `skipped_roles` reason, and two emission-only refusals (an empty phase, and `spec-coverage`)", keeping "No new flag, command, or JSON payload field." unchanged.

finding: "a corpus that has no active `spec-coverage` role produces no drop, so `tp.audit_roles` naming it takes §2.3's 'matches no active role' path, as `tp.review_roles` naming it always does" asserts a universal the role namespace does not support. Role ids are project-owned filename stems and only `regression` is reserved, so `.tp/reviewers/spec-coverage.json` is legal; `tp.review_roles` naming it then drops an active reviewer instead of taking the unknown-id path. The behaviour is still correct (the refusal is auditor-phase-only, which is right), but the rationale sentence — and §6 item 10, which pins the unknown-id path for `tp.review_roles` — is only true of corpora that happen not to use the id on the reviewer side.

resolved.evidence: §2.5's claims are scoped: the empty-phase refusal keys on the drop set, and the `spec-coverage` refusal is auditor-phase only.

suggestion: Drop "always": say that the refusal is scoped to the auditor phase because only the auditor routing depends on the id, and that a reviewer role sharing the name is deactivated like any other. Note in §6 item 10 that the assertion holds for a reviewer corpus without a `spec-coverage` role.
